title: How many floors would match the Kunchikal waterfall?
description: A person one metre tall stands beside a building of ten floors, and the building is used to feel how tall the Statue of Unity and the Kunchikal waterfall are. Keeko then raises a hand, thinking that ten floors make ten metres.
teaching_notes: One idea: a familiar object turns a huge measurement into something we can picture, and comparing means subtracting or dividing. Ask the class to say how tall one floor is before any sum is written. Watch for students who give each floor the height of the person instead of four times that height.

source: Somu is 1 m tall and each floor is about 4 m; the picture shows 10 floors; find the height of the building, how much taller the Statue of Unity (180 m) and the Kunchikal waterfall (450 m) are, and how many floors match the waterfall
video_script.why: The child can multiply, subtract and divide whole numbers and now uses them to feel how tall large heights are.
video_script.substitution: Height of a building is floors times the height of one floor, and comparing heights uses subtraction and division.
video_script.anchor: A building of ten floors stands beside a person one metre tall: how many floors would match a waterfall of four hundred fifty metres?
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko gives each floor the height of the person, one metre, so ten floors seem to make ten metres. Each floor is about four times that height, so it is four metres.
video_script.payoff_line: About one hundred thirteen floors match the waterfall

names.{{NAME_3}}: is 1 metre tall and stands beside the building of floors

never_show: a tower with a different number of floors
maths_rules: one floor is 4 × 1 = 4 m; 10 floors are 10 × 4 = 40 m
Statue of Unity: 180 − 40 = 140 m taller than the building
Kunchikal waterfall: 450 − 40 = 410 m taller than the building
floors for 450 m: 450 ÷ 4 = 112.5, so about 113 floors
the slip: ten floors make ten metres; but each floor is 4 m, so 10 floors are 40 m
video_script.design: One idea: a familiar object, a building with countable floors, makes a huge height easy to picture. Wrong idea: Keeko gives each floor the height of the person. The anchor stays all video; the working band builds in the idea part; no hard clear.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>{{NAME_3}} is one metre tall and stands beside a building of ten floors. Each floor is about four times that height.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The Kunchikal waterfall in Karnataka drops from about four hundred fifty metres.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>How many floors would the building need to be as high as the waterfall?

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>It is hard to feel how big four hundred fifty metres is on its own.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We get a better sense by comparing with something familiar.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Here the familiar thing is a building whose floors we can count.

beats.on_screen: Given: person 1 m tall; one floor is 4 times that; 10 floors; Statue of Unity 180 m; waterfall 450 m

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band
marks.m2: the two heights are added to the line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, {{NAME_3}} is one metre tall, and each floor is four times that height.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The building has ten floors. The statue is one hundred eighty metres and the waterfall is four hundred fifty metres.

beats.on_screen: To find: height of the building; how much taller the statue and the waterfall are; floors to match the waterfall

marks.m1: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find the height of the building. Then find how much taller the statue and the waterfall are.
Last, find the floors that match the waterfall.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: one floor = 4 × 1 = 4 m; building = 10 × 4 = 40 m

marks.m1: 4 × 1 = 4 m is written for one floor
marks.m2: 10 × 4 = 40 m is written for the building

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, one floor is four times one metre, which is four metres.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Ten floors make ten times four, which is forty metres.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, take the building away from the statue. One hundred eighty minus forty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The statue is one hundred forty metres taller than the building.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, take the building away from the waterfall. Four hundred fifty minus forty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The waterfall is four hundred ten metres taller than the building.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: floors = 450 ÷ 4 = 112.5, so a whole number of floors is needed
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, each floor is four metres, so divide the waterfall's height by four. Four hundred fifty divided by four.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That gives one hundred twelve and a half floors.

beats.on_screen: Answer: about 113 floors match the waterfall
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>A building cannot have half a floor, so we round up to the next whole floor.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>About one hundred thirteen floors match the waterfall.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks ten floors make ten metres, one metre for each floor.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But each floor is four times the height of {{NAME_3}}, so one floor is four metres.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Ten floors make forty metres.
